scenarios.context: Two classmates prepare for a class debate on climate change.

speakerA.en: Our teacher wants us to debate whether individuals can really make a difference to climate change.
I see your point, but if millions of people change their habits, companies have to respond to what customers want.
True, but there are cheaper choices, such as using public transport, wasting less food and buying second-hand clothes.
I agree that laws are essential. However, laws are passed because enough voters demand them.
Exactly. Neither is enough on its own, and blaming one side only delays real progress.
Which is all I'm claiming. A change in attitude often comes before a change in the rules.

speakerB.en: I'd argue that they can't. Most emissions come from big companies and governments, so recycling at home hardly matters.
That's optimistic. Many people can't afford electric cars or expensive organic food, however much they care.
Those help a little, but surely the priority should be stricter laws rather than personal guilt.
That's a fair argument. So perhaps individual action and government policy need to work together.
I'm still not convinced that small gestures are worth the effort, but I accept that they send a message.
Alright. Let's present it as a partnership and see how the class reacts.

scenarios.context: Two friends look at cheap clothes in a shop.

speakerA.en: Look at this dress. It only costs eight pounds, and it looks just like the designer version.
I hadn't thought of that. I just assumed that mass production made things cheaper.
Still, not everyone can afford expensive, ethical brands. Should they feel guilty for buying what they can afford?
I've done that before, and I was surprised by how good the quality was.
That's a good point. I've thrown away clothes after wearing them only twice.
Okay, you've convinced me. I'll put this dress back and look in the charity shop instead.

speakerB.en: That price should worry you. Someone, somewhere, is probably being paid very little to make it.
It does, but fast fashion also relies on low wages, cheap materials and a huge amount of water.
No, but there are alternatives, like second-hand shops or swapping clothes with friends.
Exactly. Buying fewer, better items also saves money in the long run.
Imagine how much waste that creates if millions of people do the same.
Great. If you find something nice, I'll come with you next time.

scenarios.context: A student asks a coordinator about volunteering at a community centre.

speakerA.en: Welcome to the community centre. Thank you for offering to volunteer with us.
That's a great attitude. We run a homework club for younger children, and we always need people who can explain things clearly.
Excellent. You'd work on Tuesdays and Thursdays from four to six, and you'd be supervised by one of our teachers.
We can be flexible during exam periods. We'd rather have a reliable volunteer for fewer hours than someone who keeps cancelling.
Yes, there's a short session about safeguarding and how to deal with difficult behaviour.
Many volunteers say that it helped them develop their patience and communication skills.

speakerB.en: I'm glad to be here. I'd like to gain experience, and I also want to give something back to the neighbourhood.
That sounds perfect. I've helped my younger brother with his maths, so I have some experience.
That's manageable, as long as it doesn't clash with my exam revision.
That's fair. Will I receive any training before I start?
Good. I'd feel much more confident knowing what to do if something went wrong.
That's exactly what I was hoping for. Where do I sign up?

scenarios.context: Two friends discuss how technology may change the job market.

speakerA.en: I read that artificial intelligence could replace millions of jobs within the next twenty years.
That's what people said about factories, but many workers suffered badly during the transition.
But who will pay for that training? Companies prefer to cut costs, and governments are slow to react.
What worries me most is that young people may find it harder to get their first job if machines do the entry-level tasks.
So it comes down to adapting. Which skills do you think will matter most?
That's comforting. Maybe schools should focus less on memorising facts and more on those skills.

speakerB.en: Some jobs will disappear, but history shows that new technology also creates new ones.
True. The real challenge is helping people retrain, rather than trying to stop progress.
Perhaps both should share the cost, since both benefit from a skilled workforce.
That's a real risk. On the other hand, those who learn to work with these tools could become far more productive.
Creativity, critical thinking and the ability to communicate with others, because those are hard to automate.
I couldn't agree more. Information is easy to find, but good judgment is much harder to replace.

scenarios.context: Two classmates debate lowering the voting age.

speakerA.en: Our class debate is about whether sixteen-year-olds should be allowed to vote. Which side are you on?
But are sixteen-year-olds mature enough? Many of them haven't even finished school or started paying taxes.
That's a fair point, but I worry that teenagers might be influenced too easily by their parents or by social media.
I like that idea. If schools prepared students properly, my objection would be much weaker.
Interesting. Do you know whether turnout among them was higher or lower than average?
In that case, I may have to rethink my position. I'd still want strong safeguards in place.

speakerB.en: I'm in favour. Decisions made today, especially about education and the climate, will affect young people longer than anyone else.
Maturity isn't guaranteed at eighteen either. Plenty of adults vote without reading anything about the candidates.
Adults are influenced too. A better solution is to teach politics and critical thinking at school so that everyone votes in an informed way.
Some countries have already lowered the voting age, and several studies suggest that young voters take it seriously.
Some studies found it was higher, probably because they were still living with their families and discussing issues at home.
That's reasonable. A good debate is about weighing the evidence, not about winning.
